newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr maintains gains vs yen on trade data in Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Dlr maintains gains vs yen on trade data in Tokyo.

text.p: The dollar maintained its gains against the yen by late Tokyo on steady buying interest on dips after earlier jumping on a smaller-than-expected Japanese customs-cleared trade surplus for June, dealers said.
But the dollar's advance versus the yen stalled somewhat in the afternoon in the absence of a strong wave of follow-through purchases.
Japan's trade surplus in June rose 27.7 percent year-on-year to 934.21 billion yen. Economists' forecasts had ranged from 971.0 billion yen to 1.61 trillion yen.
The trade surplus with the United States rose 26.8 percent year-on-year in June to 373.14 billion yen.
Interbank players and U.S. funds were said to be main buyers of dollars for yen after the data's release as they rushed to cover their short positions.
Meanwhile, Japanese investors, who have been selling dollars to hedge risks for their U.S. Treasuries holdings, also bought dollars, dealers said.

On the topside, sporadic exporter offers were detected, limiting the dollar's rise. But a city bank dealer said: "As worries about the dollar falling have disappeared, some exporters are holding back offers."
Dealers said sentiment for the dollar continues to be bullish. "If the greenback absorbs offers near 116.50 yen and breaks above that level, it could test 117 yen," a trust bank dealer said.
But aggressive follow-through purchases were lacking in the Tokyo market ahead of the release of U.S. international trade data for May due out at 1230 GMT on Friday.

Dealers were mixed on the possible impact from the U.S. trade data. "The U.S. trade data is for May, while we have already seen the result of Japan's trade data for June today. Ahead of a long weekend in Japan, the impact will be limited," the city bank dealer said.
The trust bank dealer said: "If the data shows strong figures, it will push the dollar down. But I think such a dip will only give traders a good opportunity to buy."
A comment by Andrew Card, president of the American Automobile Manufacturers' Association, that 95-105 yen is an appropriate dollar level, had a limited impact, dealers said.
"The market shrugged off his comments as Japan's trade data reduced concerns (over the U.S.-Japan trade imbalance)," the city bank dealer said.
Some traders said the market's focus may be gradually shifting from U.S.-Japan trade issues to next week's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
Dealers in Singapore said the dollar was stuck in narrow ranges against the German mark, with attention focused on the dollar/yen rate after the release of the Japanese trade data.

"Although the market had expected to hear more comments from Germany calling for a strong mark overnight, we also heard comments from a German official that the mark's weakness will stimulate the German economy. So the market is still keen to buy dollars for marks on dips," the city bank dealer said.

But another city bank dealer in Tokyo said profit-taking interest would emerge near 1.80 marks to cap the dollar's rise. The dollar closed at 115.50/60 yen and 1.7910/20 marks in New York on Wednesday.
